deck.title: Route 53
deck.analogy: DNS is the internet's phonebook: Route 53 answers the question, then exits — it never carries your traffic.

cards.front: What is Route 53 and how does DNS relate to it?

back.answer: Route 53 is AWS's DNS service; DNS is the internet's phonebook — it maps names to IP addresses.
back.explanation: You give DNS a name, it gives back a number, and then it's done. Every website visit starts with this lookup.
back.mnemonic: DNS is the internet's phonebook — name in, number out.

cards.front: Does Route 53 carry user traffic after answering a DNS query?

back.answer: No — Route 53 answers the question, then EXITS; it never carries your traffic.
back.explanation: A load balancer is a doorman in the path of every request forever; Route 53 is the lobby receptionist who points you to the right building and never sees you again.
back.mnemonic: Route 53 = receptionist (out of path); ELB = doorman (in path always).

cards.front: Route 53 vs ELB: which picks between regions and which picks between instances?

back.answer: Route 53 picks between regions or sites; the ELB picks between instances inside a region.
back.explanation: They operate at different zoom levels. Standard sandwich: User → Route 53 picks a REGION → ALB in that region picks an INSTANCE.

cards.front: Why is Route 53 failover slower than ELB failover?

back.answer: Clients cache DNS answers until TTL expires, so they keep using the old IP; the ELB is in-path and fails over instantly.
back.explanation: TTL (Time To Live) is the "how long may you remember this answer" setting. This one fact decides several exam questions.

cards.front: What does a Route 53 A record map?

back.answer: A name to an IPv4 address.

cards.front: What does a Route 53 AAAA record map?

back.answer: A name to an IPv6 address.

cards.front: What does a Route 53 CNAME record map, and where can it NOT exist?

back.answer: Maps a name to another name; it CANNOT exist at the root/apex (example.com itself) — only on subdomains like www.example.com.

cards.front: What is a Route 53 Alias record and what three advantages does it have?

back.answer: AWS extension mapping a name to an AWS resource: it WORKS at the apex, queries are free, and it auto-tracks the resource's changing IPs.
back.explanation: Alias records point at ALBs, CloudFront distributions, S3 static websites, API Gateway, and more.

cards.front: Why can you never hardcode a plain A record pointing at an ALB?

back.answer: ALB IPs change constantly, so a hardcoded A record breaks; use an Alias record that auto-tracks the IPs.
back.explanation: AWS resources like ALBs have IPs that change constantly — you can never hardcode an A record to one.

cards.front: THE trap: how do you point the root domain example.com at an ALB in Route 53?

back.answer: Alias record — never CNAME (illegal at the apex) and never a plain A record (the ALB's IPs change).
back.explanation: Root domain + AWS resource = Alias. Every time.

cards.front: What is a Route 53 hosted zone?

back.answer: A container for all the DNS records of one domain.

cards.front: Route 53 public vs private hosted zone: what is the difference?

back.answer: Public answers queries from the whole internet; private answers only from inside VPCs you attach it to.
back.explanation: Private zones give internal DNS names like db.internal.company.com that resolve only within your network.

cards.front: What does the Route 53 Simple routing policy do?

back.answer: One record, one answer, no health checks — the default; rarely the exam answer.

cards.front: What does Route 53 Weighted routing do, and what are its exam signal phrases?

back.answer: Splits traffic by percentages you assign. Signals: "A/B test", "send 10% to the new version" — canary.

cards.front: What does Route 53 Latency routing do, and what are its exam signal phrases?

back.answer: Answers with whichever region is fastest for that user. Signals: "best performance for global users", "lowest latency".

cards.front: What does Route 53 Failover routing do, and what are its exam signal phrases?

back.answer: Primary + secondary; flips when a health check fails. Signals: "active-passive", "disaster recovery site".

cards.front: What does Route 53 Geolocation routing do, and what must you not forget to create?

back.answer: Routes by where the user IS — a hard rule (compliance, language sites). Needs a Default record for unmatched locations.
back.explanation: Signal: "EU users must be served from EU" (compliance), language-specific sites.

cards.front: What does Route 53 Geoproximity routing do, and what is its name-tag signal?

back.answer: Draws a map boundary between YOUR resources, adjustable with a BIAS dial. Signals: "gradually shift/increase the traffic share to a region", the literal word "bias".

cards.front: What does Route 53 Multi-Value Answer routing do?

back.answer: Returns up to 8 healthy answers at once — "simple load balancing via DNS", a poor man's load balancer.

cards.front: Route 53 Latency vs Geolocation: how do you tell them apart on the exam?

back.answer: Latency is a performance decision (what's FASTEST for this user); Geolocation is a legal/content RULE (where the user physically is, period).
back.explanation: A user in London might get us-east-1 under Latency if it's genuinely faster; Geolocation would force German users to the German site regardless of speed.

cards.front: How do you distinguish Route 53 Geoproximity from Geolocation in a question?

back.answer: Geoproximity has a BIAS dial to expand one region's share of traffic; Geolocation has no dial — location is a fixed rule.
back.explanation: If the question says "bias" or talks about expanding one region's share by turning a dial, that's Geoproximity. Geoproximity is all dial.

cards.front: Why can't Route 53 health checks monitor private endpoints directly, and what is the fix?

back.answer: Global checkers live on the public internet and CANNOT see private endpoints; create a CloudWatch alarm for the private resource, then a health check based on that alarm.
back.explanation: Private subnets and private IPs are unreachable from the global checker fleet.

cards.front: THE trap: how do you health-check an instance with a private IP inside a VPC?

back.answer: CloudWatch alarm-based health check — global checkers can't reach it, so monitor via a CloudWatch alarm and base the check on that alarm.

cards.front: What are Route 53 calculated health checks?

back.answer: Combine up to 256 child checks with AND/OR/NOT logic into one parent check.
back.explanation: Example: "healthy only if at least 3 of 5 children are healthy".

cards.front: An instance dies inside a region — who fixes it and how fast?

back.answer: The ELB stops routing to it — instant, because the ELB is in the request path.

cards.front: A whole region or site dies — who fixes it and how fast?

back.answer: Route 53 failover policy — slow-ish, because of DNS TTL caching (clients keep the old cached IP until TTL expires).

cards.front: In a DR design with a single instance per region, why can you skip the ELB entirely?

back.answer: With nothing for an ELB to balance, Route 53 Failover pointing at the instances directly is enough — and it saves money.
back.explanation: The exam likes this corollary: single instance per region → skip the ELB.

cards.front: You must point the apex/root domain example.com at an Application Load Balancer. What do you create in Route 53?

back.answer: An Alias record pointing at the ALB.
back.explanation: CNAME is forbidden at the apex; Alias is the AWS answer, free and auto-tracking.

choices.text: Alias record pointing at the ALB
choices.why: Alias works at the apex, is free, and auto-tracks the ALB's changing IPs.

choices.text: CNAME pointing at the ALB's DNS name
choices.why: CNAME is forbidden at the root/apex — only subdomains.

choices.text: A record with the ALB's current IP addresses
choices.why: ALB IPs change constantly; a hardcoded A record breaks.

choices.text: AAAA record with the ALB's IPv6 addresses
choices.why: Same hardcoding problem — IPv6 doesn't solve apex targeting.

cards.front: An active-passive setup must send traffic to the standby region only when the primary fails. What do you configure?

back.answer: Failover routing policy + health check.
back.explanation: "Active-passive" is the giveaway for Failover routing.

choices.text: Weighted routing with weights 100 and 0
choices.why: Weighted splits by percentage for canary tests, not primary/standby failover.

choices.text: Geolocation routing to the standby region
choices.why: Geolocation routes by user location, not by failure.

choices.text: Failover routing policy with a health check on the primary
choices.why: "Active-passive" is the giveaway — primary/secondary flipped by health check.

choices.text: Multi-Value Answer routing across both regions
choices.why: Multi-Value returns several healthy answers at once, not a standby.

cards.front: You want to test a new app version by sending 10% of users to it. Which Route 53 routing policy?

back.answer: Weighted routing — canary = percentages = weights.

choices.text: Simple routing with two records
choices.why: Simple gives one answer with no percentage splitting.

choices.text: Weighted routing, 90% old and 10% new
choices.why: Canary = percentages = weights; send 10% to the new version.

choices.text: Latency routing across both versions
choices.why: Latency routes by fastest region, not by percentage.

choices.text: Failover routing with the new version as secondary
choices.why: Failover is primary/standby, not gradual percentage testing.

cards.front: Users in Germany must see the German-language site. Which Route 53 routing policy?

back.answer: Geolocation — the user's location is a RULE, not a performance choice (and don't forget the Default record).

choices.text: Latency routing
choices.why: Latency picks the fastest region, which might not serve the German site.

choices.text: Geoproximity routing with bias toward Germany
choices.why: Geoproximity shifts shares with a bias dial, not hard location rules.

choices.text: Weighted routing per country
choices.why: Weighted splits by percentage, unrelated to user location.

choices.text: Geolocation routing plus a Default record
choices.why: Location is a hard rule (language/compliance); Default catches unmatched locations.

cards.front: You must serve global users with the best possible performance. Which Route 53 routing policy?

back.answer: Latency routing — "fastest"/"best performance" = Latency.

choices.text: Latency routing
choices.why: "Best performance"/"lowest latency" — answers with the fastest region per user.

choices.text: Geolocation routing
choices.why: Geolocation is a location rule, not a performance choice.

choices.text: Multi-Value Answer routing
choices.why: Multi-Value returns healthy answers but doesn't pick the fastest.

choices.text: Weighted routing split evenly
choices.why: Weighted splits by fixed percentages, not measured speed.

cards.front: You want to gradually increase the share of traffic going to a new region. Which Route 53 feature?

back.answer: Geoproximity routing with bias — "shift traffic share" / "bias" is its name tag.

choices.text: Weighted routing updated weekly
choices.why: Weighted sets static percentages; no map boundary or bias dial.

choices.text: Geolocation routing for the new region
choices.why: Geolocation has no dial — it's a fixed location rule.

choices.text: Failover routing to the new region
choices.why: Failover flips on health checks, not gradual shifts.

choices.text: Geoproximity routing with a bias dial
choices.why: "Gradually shift/increase traffic share" and the word "bias" = Geoproximity.

cards.front: You must health-check an endpoint that has a private IP inside a VPC. How?

back.answer: CloudWatch alarm-based health check — global checkers can't see inside your VPC.

choices.text: Standard Route 53 TCP health check on the private IP
choices.why: Global checkers live on the public internet — private IPs are unreachable.

choices.text: CloudWatch alarm on the resource, then a health check based on that alarm
choices.why: The alarm monitors the private resource; the check reads the alarm state.

choices.text: Calculated health check combining the private endpoints
choices.why: Calculated checks combine children; they don't fix private reachability.

choices.text: Move the instance to a public subnet and health-check it
choices.why: Exposes the resource unnecessarily; the alarm approach keeps it private.

cards.front: You want to return several healthy IPs and let clients pick, without a load balancer. Which Route 53 policy?

back.answer: Multi-Value Answer routing — up to 8 healthy records returned at once.

choices.text: Simple routing with multiple values
choices.why: Simple returns one answer and doesn't health-check.

choices.text: Multi-Value Answer routing
choices.why: Returns up to 8 healthy records; clients pick — simple DNS-level load balancing.

choices.text: Weighted routing across all IPs
choices.why: Weighted returns one answer per percentage, not a set of healthy IPs.

choices.text: Failover routing across all IPs
choices.why: Failover returns primary (or secondary), not multiple healthy answers.

cards.front: A multi-region app needs near-INSTANT failover; DNS caching delays are unacceptable. What should you use?

back.answer: Global Accelerator instead of Route 53 — anything in the request path beats a phonebook when clients cache old answers.

choices.text: Route 53 Failover routing with very low TTLs
choices.why: Clients and resolvers cache old answers — DNS failover stays slow-ish.

choices.text: Route 53 Latency routing
choices.why: Latency optimizes speed, not instant failover.

choices.text: Route 53 Multi-Value Answer routing
choices.why: Still DNS-based — clients cache answers, so no instant cutover.

choices.text: Global Accelerator
choices.why: Stays in the request path with fixed IPs — no DNS caching delays.

cards.front: Keyword: **"Root/apex domain → ALB/CloudFront/S3"**

back.answer: Alias record

cards.front: Keyword: **"name → name, NOT at apex"**

back.answer: CNAME

cards.front: Keyword: **"A/B test", "10% canary"**

back.answer: Weighted

cards.front: Keyword: **"best performance", "lowest latency"**

back.answer: Latency

cards.front: Keyword: **"active-passive", "DR site"**

back.answer: Failover + health check

cards.front: Keyword: **"users in country X get X content", compliance**

back.answer: Geolocation (+ Default record)

cards.front: Keyword: **"bias", "shift traffic share between regions"**

back.answer: Geoproximity

cards.front: Keyword: **"up to 8 healthy answers, DNS-level LB"**

back.answer: Multi-Value

cards.front: Keyword: **"DNS only inside a VPC"**

back.answer: Private hosted zone

cards.front: Keyword: **"health check a private endpoint"**

back.answer: CloudWatch alarm-based check

cards.front: Keyword: **"combine many health checks"**

back.answer: Calculated health check

cards.front: Keyword: **"instant multi-region failover, no DNS lag"**

back.answer: Global Accelerator
